name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Tuesday 20 December 1983

clue.text: Fall in water affects the eye

definitions.note: read as 'something that affects the eye', a noun phrase

blocks.note: first meaning: a large, steep waterfall
second meaning: a clouding of the lens that dims sight

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a warning about splashing water in your eyes, but it is two separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a great waterfall and the eye condition in which the lens turns cloudy.

clue.text: Canvasser in badly organised race about who wins the election?

indicators.note: badly organised means put in a muddled order, so the next word is shuffled
about means surrounding, so the muddled word goes around the electoral winner

blocks.note: the winner of a British parliamentary election becomes a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A political canvasser in a chaotic contest wonders who will take the seat.
explanation.walkthrough: A canvasser seems to be an election doorknocker; here it is someone who sleeps under canvas.
explanation.definitionFit: A camper sleeps in a tent, which is made of canvas, so a humorous 'canvasser'.

clue.text: He leaves the corner in con fusion

indicators.note: when someone leaves they are gone, so those letters are taken out

blocks.note: taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: A man walks away from the street corner in a muddle over a swindle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Con fusion' is confusion split in two, so the clue defines a muddle; 'He' is not the man in the scene but two letters to strike out.
explanation.definitionFit: A tangle is a confused, muddled state, just as confusion is.

clue.text: Where holidaymakers shuffle about again?

definitions.note: a verb, read as one word split in two

blocks.note: second meaning: sort a second time, with a hyphen after the first two letters

explanation.walkthrough: Hyphenated, the word means to sort once more, as with shuffled cards.
explanation.definitionFit: A resort is a place people visit on holiday, and re-sort is to arrange again.

clue.text: Craftsmen - those who carry about drawing equipment

indicators.note: about means around, so the carriers' word wraps the drawing tool

blocks.note: a pen is used for drawing

explanation.surface: Tradesmen are described as people who lug drafting tools around.
explanation.definitionFit: Carpenters are woodworkers, skilled tradesmen who work timber by hand.

clue.text: Rings shone nicely after a bit of polish

indicators.note: a bit of a word is only a small piece of it, here its opening letter
done nicely suggests arranged neatly, so the word before it is set out in a new order
after places the rearranged word behind the single letter in the answer

explanation.surface: A ring sparkles nicely once someone has given it a little polish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rings' looks like jewellery that shone after polishing, but it is the verb: telephones someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To ring someone is to telephone them, so 'rings' and 'phones' are interchangeable verbs.

clue.text: Given out between Hammersmith and Billingsgate?

indicators.note: between says the answer lies across the gap separating the two place names

blocks.note: the end of the first name, the joining word and the start of the second, run together

explanation.surface: Something is distributed among the districts of west and east London.
explanation.walkthrough: Hammersmith and Billingsgate are London districts, Billingsgate long home to the fish market. 'Given out' is a noun phrase here: a thing that is given out.
explanation.definitionFit: A handbill is a small printed leaflet distributed by hand in the street.

clue.text: Advice to the overweight - strain one's stew!

indicators.note: to strain is to force out of shape, so the letters that follow are bent into a new order

explanation.surface: A dieting tip: sieve the fat out of your casserole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strain' looks like kitchen advice to drain the stew, but it signals the letters are mixed.
explanation.definitionFit: Telling dieters to give up confectionery and desserts is classic slimming advice.

clue.text: Clean remark about Art in transition

indicators.note: in transition means changing form, so the two words before it change their order
about means around, so the word for remark wraps the changed letters

explanation.surface: A neat comment on how art is changing.
explanation.definitionFit: Sanitary means hygienic and free from dirt, a synonym for clean.

clue.text: Clergy reveals one's attempt to follow the road north

indicators.note: to follow puts the second group of words after the first in the answer

blocks.note: the M1, Britain's first motorway, written with I for 1
one is I, so one's is I'S

explanation.surface: A clergyman sets off up the main road north, making a brave attempt at the journey.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the motorway running north from London; crosswords write it MI.
explanation.definitionFit: The ministry is the body of ordained clergy collectively, as in 'entering the ministry'.

clue.text: Spithead enters the brotherhood in concert

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, here the word fused to it
something that enters goes inside, so one letter goes into the word that follows

blocks.note: a brotherhood is a union, as of workers
read as spit-head, the opening letter of spit

explanation.surface: Spithead, the naval anchorage off Portsmouth, seemingly joins a fraternity performing together.
explanation.walkthrough: Spithead is a real stretch of water off Portsmouth, so the place name hides the instruction 'head of spit'.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting in unison means acting together as one, just as performers in concert do.

clue.text: Way out of Greenland blown up?

indicators.note: way out means wildly unconventional, so the following place name is jumbled

blocks.note: the island's name taken as written, except that one of its two Ns has no place in the answer

explanation.surface: Someone asks what route leads out of Greenland, perhaps after an explosion.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder has one N too many for the eight-letter answer, a slip by the setter; the remaining letters rearrange to ENLARGED.
explanation.definitionFit: A photograph that is blown up has been made bigger, which is what enlarged means.

clue.text: Seaman posted missing

explanation.surface: A sailor has been officially listed as missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Posted missing' sounds like a naval casualty notice, but posted is just SENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone missing is not present, which is what absent means.

clue.text: I have to follow primate as ordered - it's a must!

indicators.note: as ordered means arranged to instructions, so the word for ape is set in a new order
to follow puts the first words after the rearranged primate

explanation.surface: Someone is told they must come after an archbishop as instructed, no choice.
explanation.walkthrough: A primate is also a senior archbishop, which helps the surface; here it is only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something imperative is absolutely necessary, so it is a must.

clue.text: I strum a lot - this way I get folks moving

indicators.note: this way invites the solver to set the preceding words out in a different arrangement

explanation.surface: A guitarist boasts that heavy strumming gets the crowd dancing.
explanation.definitionFit: A stimulator is anything that rouses people into activity, getting them going.

clue.text: Weightlifter to take away a girl's breath?

definitions.text: to take away a girl's breath?
definitions.note: read as the phrase 'wind lass', a verb and its object

blocks.note: first meaning: a winch for hauling up heavy loads

blocks.clueFragment: to take away a girl's breath?
blocks.note: second meaning: to wind a young woman, punching the breath out of her

explanation.walkthrough: To wind someone is to knock the breath out of them, and a lass is a girl; split, the word is that phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A windlass is a cranked drum winch used for hoisting anchors or buckets, so it lifts weights.

clue.text: Qualified communication to the boss?

blocks.note: a letter is a written communication
ED, the editor, is the boss of a newspaper

explanation.surface: A properly worded memo addressed to one's manager.
explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords the boss of a paper is the editor, ED.
explanation.definitionFit: Lettered means educated, holding qualifications or letters after one's name.

clue.text: Clanger about commercial piece of writing-up - evidently there's something rotten

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from bottom to top
about means around, so the clanger wraps the other pieces

blocks.note: a bell is something that clangs

explanation.surface: A blunder in an advertising write-up shows something is badly wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: A clanger is British slang for a blunder, but here it is literally something that clangs.
explanation.definitionFit: A foul odour is the obvious sign that something has gone off, so it shows rot.

clue.text: Playwright scatters rice — it holds up polar progress

indicators.note: to scatter is to throw things about, so the letters land in a new order

blocks.note: J. M. Barrie, Scottish author of Peter Pan

explanation.surface: A dramatist throws rice about at a wedding, while elsewhere an expedition is stalled.
explanation.walkthrough: The playwright's name and rice are jumbled together as one batch of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An ice barrier is a wall of ice, such as the Antarctic shelf, that blocks explorers heading for the Pole.

clue.text: Snakes and ladders novice lost

indicators.note: something lost is gone, so that letter is dropped from the word

explanation.surface: A beginner loses at the board game snakes and ladders.
explanation.walkthrough: Snakes and ladders is the children's board game; 'snakes' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Adders are vipers, the venomous snakes of Britain.

clue.text: Discovery of offal condemned a bird .. .

indicators.note: dis-covery read as removing a cover, taking the word of off what follows it

blocks.note: taken as written, with of to be removed
a con, convict, is a condemned person

explanation.surface: Someone finds animal innards and declares a bird unfit to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovery of' removes the letters OF from the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: A falcon is a bird of prey, used in falconry for hunting.

clue.text: ... hatched out of the sun

blocks.note: first meaning: drawn with fine lines to give tone

explanation.walkthrough: The dots join it to the bird of the clue before, so 'hatched' looks like a chick; it means drawn with lines.
explanation.definitionFit: Hatching shades a drawing with parallel lines, and a shaded spot is one sheltered from sunlight.

clue.text: Hate to be half-dead at the trial

indicators.note: half of a word keeps just one of its halves, here the front two letters

explanation.surface: Someone loathes being left exhausted by a court hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: The newspaper scan reads 'Hale', but the definition must be 'Hate'. 'Trial' suggests a courtroom; here it means a test.
explanation.definitionFit: To detest something is to loathe it intensely, a stronger synonym for hate.

clue.text: Stumped up, ordering chaps to gather help

indicators.note: ordering means putting into a fresh sequence, so the word after it is rearranged
to gather is to draw something in, so the rearranged word wraps around another

explanation.surface: Someone paid up under orders, making the men gather assistance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stumped up' is British slang for handing over money, often reluctantly.
explanation.definitionFit: To stump up is to pay money over, and paying cash is settling the bill in notes and coins.

clue.text: They need atmosphere to work in

definitions.text: They need atmosphere to work in

blocks.clueFragment: They need atmosphere to work in
blocks.note: surface reading: people such as actors or artists who need the right mood to work
setter's reading: the literal air of the sky, where these people do their job

explanation.walkthrough: Atmosphere suggests ambience or mood; taken literally it is the air, the workplace of fliers.
explanation.definitionFit: Airmen are aviators, members of an air force, and they fly through the atmosphere.

clue.text: Declines incorrectly and not allowed to speak

indicators.note: something done incorrectly is wrongly arranged, so the word before is put right in another order

explanation.surface: Someone who refuses badly finds they have been gagged.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone silenced has been forbidden or prevented from talking.

clue.text: A seat on the hill . . .

definitions.note: read as 'a feature on the hill'

blocks.note: first meaning: the seat a rider sits on
second meaning: a dip in a ridge between two summits

explanation.walkthrough: The dots run on into the next clue, where the hill has grass and a boy, but this answer stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A rider's leather seat and a low col along a ridge share one name, from the ridge's shape.

clue.text: . . . where a boy in the grass argued

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another, here inside a word for a kind of grass

blocks.note: a reed is a tall waterside grass
a boy is a son, kept with its article

explanation.surface: Continuing a hillside scene, a lad lying in the grass is making his case.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading dots tie it to the clue before, but the wordplay is complete on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: To reason with someone is to argue logically, so reasoned works for argued.
